# dbplyr {#sec-dbplyr}

## Introduction

In this chapter, we will learn to query data from a database using dplyr.

We will use the following R packages:

- [DBI](https://dbi.r-dbi.org/)
- [RSQLite](https://rsqlite.r-dbi.org/)
- [dbplyr](http://dbplyr.tidyverse.org/)
- [dplyr](http://dplyr.tidyverse.org/)

```{r lite1a, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE, results='hide', message=FALSE}
library(dbplyr)
library(dplyr)
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
```

All the data sets used in this chapter can be found [here](https://github.com/rsquaredacademy/datasets) and code can be downloaded from [here](https://gist.github.com/aravindhebbali/f5ee72cee9ab3256230cdedecd3ef25b) or run from `code/ch2-dbplyr.R` in this repo.

## Connect to Database

Let us connect to an in memory SQLite database using `dbConnect()`.

```{r dbply1}
con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
```

We will copy the `ecom` data to the database so that we can use it for running
dplyr statements. We read the same `ecom` data set used across chapters
(1000 rows, 8 columns including `country` and `purchase`) from the local
`data/web.csv` snapshot, falling back to the online copy if needed.

```{r dbply2, message=FALSE}
web_path <- if (file.exists("data/web.csv")) "data/web.csv" else "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rsquaredacademy/datasets/master/web.csv"
ecom <- readr::read_csv(web_path, show_col_types = FALSE)
ecom <- dplyr::select(ecom, referrer, device, bouncers, n_visit, n_pages, duration, country, purchase)
dplyr::copy_to(con, ecom)
```

## Reference Data 

In order to use dplyr functions, we need to reference the table in the database using
`tbl()`.

```{r dbply3}
ecom2 <- dplyr::tbl(con, "ecom")
ecom2
```

## Query Data 

We will look at some simple examples. Let us start by selecting `referrer`, `device` and `duration` 
columns from `ecom2`.

```{r dbply4}
select(ecom2, referrer, device, duration)
```

We can filter data as well. Filter all the rows from `ecom2` where `duration` 
is greater than 300.

```{r dbply5}
filter(ecom2, duration > 300)
```

Time to do some grouping and summarizing. Let us compute the average time spent
on the site for different types of devices.

```{r dbply6}
ecom2 %>%
  group_by(device) %>%
  summarise(avg_duration = mean(duration))
```

## Show Query

If you want to view the SQL query generated in the above step, use `show_query()` or `explain()`.

```{r dbply7, collapse=TRUE}
avg_time <- 
  ecom2 %>%
  group_by(device) %>%
  summarise(avg_duration = mean(duration))

dplyr::show_query(avg_time)

dplyr::explain(avg_time)
```

## Collect Data

Now, some interesting facts. When working with databases, **dplyr** never pulls data into R unless you explicitly ask for it. In the previous example, dplyr will not do anything until you ask for the `avg_time` data. It generates the SQL and only pulls down a few rows when you try to print `avg_time`. 
So how do we pull all the data and store it for further analysis? `collect()` will pull all 
the data and store it in a tibble and you can use it for any further analysis.

```{r dbply9}
dplyr::collect(avg_time)
```

We can also combine tables with R verbs, as in the SQL joins in @sec-joins.
The examples below use a separate customer and order dataset from
`data/ecom.sqlite`: 20 customers and 20 orders, including six customers
with no orders. Let us load those tables into this connection:

```{r dbplyr-join-setup, include=FALSE}
join_source <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "data/ecom.sqlite")
DBI::dbWriteTable(con, "customers", DBI::dbReadTable(join_source, "customers"))
DBI::dbWriteTable(con, "orders", DBI::dbReadTable(join_source, "orders"))
DBI::dbDisconnect(join_source)
```

## JOINs with dbplyr

The same joins work from R without writing SQL. Reference both tables and use
the dplyr join verbs:

```{r join-dbplyr, message=FALSE}
customers <- dplyr::tbl(con, "customers")
orders <- dplyr::tbl(con, "orders")

inner_join(customers, orders, by = "customer_id")
```

Use `show_query()` to see the SQL dbplyr generates -- it is the `INNER JOIN`
you just wrote by hand:

```{r join-show-inner, collapse=TRUE}
q_inner <- inner_join(customers, orders, by = "customer_id")
dplyr::show_query(q_inner)
```

The left join works the same way:

```{r join-show-left, collapse=TRUE}
q_left <- left_join(customers, orders, by = "customer_id")
dplyr::show_query(q_left)
```

## semi_join and anti_join

Two filtering joins have no direct SQL keyword but are everyday tools:

- `semi_join()` keeps rows of `customers` that **have** a match in `orders`
  (14 customers). The generated SQL uses `WHERE EXISTS`.
- `anti_join()` keeps rows of `customers` that **lack** a match in `orders`
  (the same 6 customers from the `LEFT JOIN` check above). The generated SQL
  uses `WHERE NOT EXISTS`.

```{r join-semi, collapse=TRUE}
q_semi <- semi_join(customers, orders, by = "customer_id")
dplyr::show_query(q_semi)
dplyr::collect(q_semi)
```

```{r join-anti, collapse=TRUE}
q_anti <- anti_join(customers, orders, by = "customer_id")
dplyr::show_query(q_anti)
dplyr::collect(q_anti)
```

Rule of thumb: use `semi_join()` / `anti_join()` when you want to filter one
table by membership in another without adding the other table's columns.

It is good practice to close the connection when you are done:

```{r dbply-close}
dbDisconnect(con)
```
